title: Eddie Oliver, Herman Vernon and Doc Ross's Rendezvous Club band
summary: Manno talks about Kelly-influenced pianist Eddie Oliver, the late fiddler Herman Vernon, and the members of Doc Ross's Houston band including Kit Reed and Skipper Trevathan.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Chris Kelly, the blues trumpeter and his band

blocks.x: well the closest that we had to pet Kelly down there was a boy by the name of Eddie Oliver now there there are a whole bunch of Eddie Oliver's there was an Eddie Oliver that was with the old Ben Bernie band and there was another Eddie Oliver over in Beaumont somewhere but this one was from Houston incidentally he's in Chicago now but he played very much like peck he was influenced by peck but while he did play very much like peck there was only one Kelly no and and and and like and like all of these fellas you know peck peck was a character he had his on nights and off nights and he had more off nights and he had on nights and if he felt like playing well he played and nothing in creation would hold him back but if he didn't want to play money or anything else wouldn't make him play it just depend on whether he wanted to we were talking about Herman Vernon this afternoon too oh well Herman was originally a member of the Houston local he was a piano man and a fiddle man here several weeks ago we got a notice at the Union that he had died here in New Orleans in jail and we did know that Herman was a pretty heavy drinker and he was on marijuana dope just everything but he was a real talent he played real fine jazz piano and he probably played the dirtiest hot fiddle of anyone I've ever heard it seems like all jazz fiddle players they have some characteristic violinistic touch that doesn't lend itself to jazz and Herman didn't have that he sounded like he was playing a horn and that's the thing that seemed to make him so outstanding to everyone that hurt him but it's very unfortunate that a man with all those talents has to end up that way but I guess it isn't the first time it's happened and I'm sure it won't be the last time did you ever hear Doc Ross's band I remember Doc Ross band when he had the rendezvous club in Houston that was located out on South Main and Dryden but they closed up the rendezvous club it must have been around 36 or 37 I would say 37 would be stretching it and that's the last time and that's the last I've heard of Doc did you know any of the fellows in his band well Felix Stagno was a guitar and banjo player with Doc and Richard Shannon played sax clarinet and xylophone that was before they started using vibraphone he also had a trombone player by the name of Howard Stratton he plays around town here you knew how it's fatten I don't know him I can never find him he's always out on the road he died he dead and Kit Reed played some now incidentally Kit Reed was about as fine a trumpet man as you ever hope to hear in fact Kit still plays awful good but he's a little bit dated he's from the same vintage as Goodman and Shaw and Woody Herman and those boys like that and he hasn't kept up with the times as much as they have and his playing is still back from the middle 30s and he was with Doc and Doc's bass player was Ray Potts and last I heard of Ray he was a bank teller somewhere up in Memphis I can't remember I can't remember Oh Skipper Trevathan played piano with him incidentally old Skipper is one of the finest blues piano players that I've ever heard too he plays and sings blues and he has a style that the minute he that you hear him it's skipper and it's nobody else but skipper he incorporates a certain flavor and everything that he does whether it's blues or not it still has the blues flavor Trevathan style

Doc was a drummer however Doc didn't always play he hired a drummer to be on the stand whenever he wanted to get off and I was trying to remember who played drums for Doc if I'm not mistaken I think Pat Quinn played some drums for Doc now whether he was his regular drummer I don't know
